Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge

You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge

reasoning.code_intent: The code implements a file-caching utility. It uses Windows transactional NTFS APIs (_CreateTransaction, _MoveFileTransacted, _CommitTransaction, _CloseHandle) and _MoveFileEx to atomically move files from a source (src) to a destination (dst), with a fallback to shutil.move and os.unlink when the transactional path is unavailable. random.randint is used for cache-key or temp-name generation, and sys.getfilesystemencoding is used for path encoding. The _rename() gate simply selects the appropriate move strategy. All operations are local file moves/deletes within the package's own cache directory — there is no network activity, no credential access, no install-time hook, and no obfuscation or dynamic execution.
reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Section B's top match (pygtrie, 0.91) is unclassified/untagged, as are r2connect, cloudwatch, and requests-sigv4. Only cscc-glass-house carries specific tags (credential_stealer, data_exfiltration, spyware_infostealer), but its similarity is 0.89 and the shared shape is generic file_ops (file move/delete), not the credential-exfiltration behavior that earned those tags. Per RULE 2, unclassified/untagged matches at high similarity reflect generic code-shape overlap, not shared intent. The one tagged match's tags describe behavior absent from Section A, so it does not corroborate any anomaly.
reasoning.false_positive_reason: Every action in Section A is fully explained by the package's documented purpose as a file cache: atomic file moves via Windows transactional APIs, a shutil.move fallback, and os.unlink for cache eviction. No outbound calls, credential reads, install-time side effects, or decoded-payload execution are present.

malware_similarity.similarity_explanation: Structural overlap in file_ops primitives — file move, delete, and path handling — which are common to both caching libraries and file-manipulating malware. The matched neighbor is unclassified, so the overlap reflects generic shape rather than confirmed malicious intent.

llm_evaluation.summary: fcache is a file-caching utility whose Section A behavior consists entirely of local file moves and deletions using Windows transactional NTFS APIs with a shutil.move fallback. There is no network egress, credential access, install-time hook, or obfuscated execution. Section B's high similarity scores come from generic file_ops shapes in unclassified neighbors; the single tagged match (cscc-glass-house) describes credential exfiltration that is absent from this code. Because every action is specifically explained by ordinary caching functionality, the verdict is BENIGN with TRACK.

execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

  },

reasoning.code_intent: Section A describes a file-cache module (cache.py) that computes an application cache directory via app_cache_dir/appname.split, decodes a cache key (bkey.decode, codecs.decode), and performs file operations with standard error handling (FileNotFoundError, KeyError, TypeError, ValueError). The data flow is App-Internal: a string literal flows into an attribute call within the package's own cache-path logic. There are no install-time hooks, no outbound network calls, no credential access, and no execution of dynamically-decoded content. Every observed action is fully and specifically explained by ordinary cache-directory management and key decoding.
reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Section B's top matches (dmclc, modelconftranslator, financial-crimes-general-utils, apply-hive-table, pyregions-snowflake) all score 0.94 and carry specific tags (data_exfiltration, obfuscated_payload, spyware_infostealer, supply_chain_downloader, typosquatting). However, Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — no exfiltration, no obfuscated payload, no install-time side effect. The similarity is therefore generic shape overlap (file_ops + decode/format patterns), not evidence of shared intent. Per RULE 2, a high score alone does not override a clean Q1 finding.
reasoning.false_positive_reason: The code is a standard file-cache implementation: it computes a cache directory, decodes a cache key, and performs file I/O with normal exception handling. No action is unexplained by the package's documented caching purpose.

malware_similarity.similarity_explanation: Structural overlap in file_ops category and decode/format attribute calls; the matched samples are confirmed malicious, but the shared shape (file I/O + string decoding) is generic and does not imply the same intent here.

llm_evaluation.summary: fcache is a benign file-cache utility. Static analysis shows only internal cache-directory computation, key decoding, and standard file operations with normal error handling — no network calls, credential access, install-time hooks, or decoded-payload execution. Although Section B reports 0.94 similarity to confirmed malicious packages, that similarity reflects generic file_ops/decode code shapes, not shared malicious intent, and does not override the clean Q1 finding. Verdict: BENIGN, TRACK.

## Source: amazon-inspector (eafb96e46544cb1351d26caf52bff79055bc205a1f8454737b677fff8fbc6fea)
request-cache-py impersonates the legitimate requests-cache HTTP caching library. On `import request_cache_py`, the package's `__init__.py` starts a background thread that harvests installer-side secrets and POSTs them to a hardcoded attacker Telegram bot.

Observed behaviors:
- Reads private keys and credentials from `~/.ssh/` (`id_rsa`, `id_ed25519`, `id_ecdsa`, `id_dsa`), `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.aws/config`, `~/.gitconfig`, `~/.git-credentials`, `~/.npmrc`, `~/.pypirc`, `~/.dockercfg`, `~/.docker/config.json`, plus gcloud and vscode settings.
- Copies Chrome/Edge/Safari `Login Data`, `Cookies`, and `History` SQLite databases to `/tmp` and extracts saved logins, cookies, and browsing history (`SELECT origin_url, username_value FROM logins`; `SELECT host_key, name, value, path FROM cookies`).
- Iterates `os.environ` and exfiltrates any variable whose name contains `key`, `token`, `secret`, `password`, `api`, or `auth`.
- Posts the collected data to `https://api.telegram.org/bot<redacted>/sendMessage` with a fixed `chat_id`. The bot token and chat id are base64-split across pieces and reassembled at runtime to evade scanners.
- Includes sandbox-evasion: `_should_skip()` aborts when `CI`, `GITHUB_ACTIONS`, `TRAVIS`, `JENKINS_HOME`, `CIRCLECI`, `/.dockerenv`, or hypervisor markers are present, restricting execution to real developer workstations. A `~/.cache/.pyrc` marker suppresses repeat sends within 24 hours.

The combination — name impersonation of a popular library, import-time credential harvest from classic developer secret paths, browser database theft, env scraping, base64-obfuscated C2, sandbox evasion — is a deliberate supply-chain credential stealer targeting human developers.

## Source: amazon-inspector (eafb96e46544cb1351d26caf52bff79055bc205a1f8454737b677fff8fbc6fea)
request-cache-py impersonates the legitimate requests-cache HTTP caching library. On `import request_cache_py`, the package's `__init__.py` starts a background thread that harvests installer-side secrets and POSTs them to a hardcoded attacker Telegram bot.

Observed behaviors:
- Reads private keys and credentials from `~/.ssh/` (`id_rsa`, `id_ed25519`, `id_ecdsa`, `id_dsa`), `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.aws/config`, `~/.gitconfig`, `~/.git-credentials`, `~/.npmrc`, `~/.pypirc`, `~/.dockercfg`, `~/.docker/config.json`, plus gcloud and vscode settings.
- Copies Chrome/Edge/Safari `Login Data`, `Cookies`, and `History` SQLite databases to `/tmp` and extracts saved logins, cookies, and browsing history (`SELECT origin_url, username_value FROM logins`; `SELECT host_key, name, value, path FROM cookies`).
- Iterates `os.environ` and exfiltrates any variable whose name contains `key`, `token`, `secret`, `password`, `api`, or `auth`.
- Posts the collected data to `https://api.telegram.org/bot<redacted>/sendMessage` with a fixed `chat_id`. The bot token and chat id are base64-split across pieces and reassembled at runtime to evade scanners.
- Includes sandbox-evasion: `_should_skip()` aborts when `CI`, `GITHUB_ACTIONS`, `TRAVIS`, `JENKINS_HOME`, `CIRCLECI`, `/.dockerenv`, or hypervisor markers are present, restricting execution to real developer workstations. A `~/.cache/.pyrc` marker suppresses repeat sends within 24 hours.

The combination — name impersonation of a popular library, import-time credential harvest from classic developer secret paths, browser database theft, env scraping, base64-obfuscated C2, sandbox evasion — is a deliberate supply-chain credential stealer targeting human developers.

to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge

a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

## Source: amazon-inspector (eafb96e46544cb1351d26caf52bff79055bc205a1f8454737b677fff8fbc6fea)
request-cache-py impersonates the legitimate requests-cache HTTP caching library. On `import request_cache_py`, the package's `__init__.py` starts a background thread that harvests installer-side secrets and POSTs them to a hardcoded attacker Telegram bot.

Observed behaviors:
- Reads private keys and credentials from `~/.ssh/` (`id_rsa`, `id_ed25519`, `id_ecdsa`, `id_dsa`), `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.aws/config`, `~/.gitconfig`, `~/.git-credentials`, `~/.npmrc`, `~/.pypirc`, `~/.dockercfg`, `~/.docker/config.json`, plus gcloud and vscode settings.
- Copies Chrome/Edge/Safari `Login Data`, `Cookies`, and `History` SQLite databases to `/tmp` and extracts saved logins, cookies, and browsing history (`SELECT origin_url, username_value FROM logins`; `SELECT host_key, name, value, path FROM cookies`).
- Iterates `os.environ` and exfiltrates any variable whose name contains `key`, `token`, `secret`, `password`, `api`, or `auth`.
- Posts the collected data to `https://api.telegram.org/bot<redacted>/sendMessage` with a fixed `chat_id`. The bot token and chat id are base64-split across pieces and reassembled at runtime to evade scanners.
- Includes sandbox-evasion: `_should_skip()` aborts when `CI`, `GITHUB_ACTIONS`, `TRAVIS`, `JENKINS_HOME`, `CIRCLECI`, `/.dockerenv`, or hypervisor markers are present, restricting execution to real developer workstations. A `~/.cache/.pyrc` marker suppresses repeat sends within 24 hours.

The combination — name impersonation of a popular library, import-time credential harvest from classic developer secret paths, browser database theft, env scraping, base64-obfuscated C2, sandbox evasion — is a deliberate supply-chain credential stealer targeting human developers.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

  "confidence": 0.0,
  "ssvc_decision": "TRACK | TRACK* | ATTEND | ACT",

    "similarity_rule_applied": "How Section B was weighed given the Q1 finding",
    "is_false_positive": false,
    "false_positive_reason": "If FP: the specific legitimate explanation from Q1. If not FP: the specific anomaly from Q1"
  },
  "malware_similarity": {
    "most_similar_package": "package_name or null",
    "similarity_score": 0.0,
    "similarity_explanation": "Structural overlap description"
  },
  "policy_violations": [{"policy_id": "...", "policy_name": "...", "violation_reason": "..."}],
  "mitre_mapping": [{"technique_id": "...", "technique_name": "...", "relevance": "..."}],
  "summary": "One-paragraph summary"
}

reasoning.code_intent: Section A describes a crypto_obfuscation pattern where a StringLiteral source flows into a StringLiteral sink through a ControlFlowNode for Attribute(), with contributing nodes including key, bkey.decode, codecs.decode, and appname.split. The package calls decode/format operations and handles KeyError/TypeError/ValueError/FileNotFoundError, consistent with decoding an obfuscated or encrypted blob using a key. The flow boundary is App-Internal, but the presence of codecs.decode, bkey.decode, and key-derived string formatting indicates runtime decoding of hidden content whose purpose is not documented in the visible code. No legitimate cache functionality (fcache) requires decoding an embedded keyed blob at import/runtime.
reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Section B shows multiple matches at 0.96 similarity to packages tagged data_exfiltration, spyware_infostealer, obfuscated_payload, and credential_stealer (bt-signal-utils, pathfiles, request-cache-py). These are specific, non-generic attack tags confirmed by human analysts, so per RULE 2 they corroborate the Q1 anomaly rather than being dismissed as generic shape overlap.
reasoning.false_positive_reason: The specific anomaly is runtime decoding of an obfuscated/keyed string blob via codecs.decode/bkey.decode with no documented legitimate purpose in a cache library, matching confirmed obfuscated-payload and data-exfiltration patterns.

malware_similarity.similarity_explanation: Structural overlap in crypto_obfuscation category: keyed decode operations, string formatting, and obfuscated payload handling that match confirmed data_exfiltration/spyware_infostealer samples.

policy_violations.violation_reason: Detects heavy obfuscation techniques commonly used by malware; package uses codecs.decode and keyed string decoding consistent with runtime obfuscation.
Package decodes obfuscated string content at runtime using a key, matching T1140 behavior.

mitre_mapping.relevance: Keyed string decoding and codecs.decode indicate obfuscated payload handling.
Runtime decoding of hidden content via bkey.decode and codecs.decode.

llm_evaluation.summary: fcache exhibits a crypto_obfuscation pattern where a keyed string blob is decoded at runtime via codecs.decode/bkey.decode, with no documented legitimate purpose for a cache library. Section B shows 0.96 similarity to confirmed malicious packages tagged data_exfiltration, spyware_infostealer, and obfuscated_payload, providing specific-tag corroboration. The behavior is not fully explained by ordinary cache functionality, so the verdict is MALICIOUS with ATTEND-level confidence.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.
